slides.title: The account, opened up
slides.notes: Open on the number, not the pleasantries. The whole deck is built to answer one question: what did the spend buy? The honest answer is that nobody can currently say, and that is the finding worth paying to fix.

blocks.text: ALTTRED NEXXUS  ×  GUHANTARA
A full audit of the brand, the website, the Meta account and the Google account — and what ₹45.65 lakh actually bought.
1 January 2025 – 29 September 2026
Prepared 29 September 2026

slides.title: What we looked at
slides.notes: Establish standing before making claims. The last card is the pivot: the biggest thing we could not audit is the thing they most need built.

blocks.text: The accounts
The property
21 months of Meta, broken out by month, age, gender, platform and placement. 19 months of Google, by month and by campaign type. Same window for both.
The website, the booking engine, live room rates, 21,392 Google reviews, 317 TripAdvisor reviews and the twenty competing resorts on Kanakapura Road.
The category
What we could not see
Hospitality social benchmarks for 2025–26, Indian travel discovery research, and how the properties that command a premium are positioned.
Any CRM, because there is none. Any booking data, because none is captured. Which is the finding, not a gap in the audit.
Every figure in this deck comes from the client's own accounts or a named public source.

slides.title: Guhantara has the demand of a category leader, the positioning of a commodity, and no way to tell which of its rupees worked.
slides.notes: This is the slide the room should remember. Say it once, pause, move on. Do not soften it: they already suspect it, which is why we were asked for this audit.

Three problems, one root. Everything that follows is evidence for that sentence and a plan to change it.

slides.title: The awareness is already won. The reputation is being lost.
slides.notes: The complaints are consistent and they are all one complaint: too many people on peak days. Overcrowding, hygiene slipping, buffet queues, prices that feel high for what arrives. The praise is equally consistent: food variety, staff, rain dance, tunnel trek.

rated it two stars or less. That is 15% of everyone who walked through the door and wrote about it.
Against 726 ratings for Wild Valley and 754 for Elim, Guhantara has roughly 25 times the reviewed footfall of its nearest neighbours on the same road.
TripAdvisor ranks it #587 of 1,258 Bengaluru hotels. Value 3.1. Service 3.1.

slides.title: Half the budget: ₹7,41,739 spent with no lead recorded
slides.notes: Do not let this be heard as "your agency wasted half the money". Say it precisely: half the spend ran through periods where the account was not set up to record an outcome, so nobody can say whether it worked. The honest version is more damning and more fixable.

blocks.text: HALF THE BUDGET
In the eleven months where leads were tracked, the same account delivered 1,259 leads at ₹597 each. The tracking, not the media, is what changed.
Months with zero leads recorded: Jan, Feb, Mar, Apr, Aug, Oct, Nov 2025 and Apr, May, Jun 2026.

slides.notes: The pattern is not gradual decline. It is on-and-off tracking. Point at the run of rust bars in mid-2026 and note that spend was heavy in exactly those months.

slides.title: Cost per lead swings by a factor of 393
slides.notes: January 2026 is the proof that the media can work: 242 leads at 236 rupees. Use it as the benchmark we intend to return to, not as a stick.

blocks.text: A resort's audience does not become 393 times harder to reach in two months. This is a measurement artefact, not a market shift, and it makes every optimisation decision taken on this data unsafe.
Selected months. Best recorded month ₹236, worst ₹92,713.

slides.title: Two thirds of the clicks you pay for never arrive
slides.notes: This is the single most commercially significant number in the Meta audit. It is also the cheapest to fix, and the fix is mostly on the website, not in the ad account.

blocks.text: Bare minimum
Outbound clicks that became a landing page view
60–70%. Below this, the page or the pixel is the problem, not the audience.
Healthy
Above 80%. The click, the page and the measurement are all doing their job.
Across the full 21 months and ₹14.94L of spend.
Where Guhantara sits
33.72%. Two out of every three paid clicks are either bouncing before the page loads or not being recorded at all.
On ₹14.94L of spend, closing the gap to 70% is worth more than any creative change in this deck.
OBC>LPV = outbound clicks to landing page views. Source: Meta Ads Manager.

slides.title: October 2025: 133.33% of clicks became page views
slides.notes: Keep this slide short and let the number sit. If anyone in the room defends the current setup, this is the number that ends the argument without anyone needing to be blamed.

blocks.text: OCTOBER 2025
of outbound clicks became landing page views. More people arrived at the page than left the advert to get there.

That is arithmetically impossible, and it is the cleanest single proof that the measurement is broken. In the same 21 months the figure ranges from 0.01% in January 2025 to this. Neither end is a real audience behaviour.
Source: Meta Ads Manager monthly export, OBC>LPV column.

slides.title: Money spent where nothing has ever converted
slides.notes: This is the easiest win in the deck and it can be actioned the same afternoon. Do not oversell it; it is worth less than the OBC fix.

blocks.text: Across four placements and platforms
and not one recorded lead in 21 months.

Audience Network and Threads rarely produce a result for any brand we run, so the honest move is to exclude them outright and cap anything similar to a token share of budget. Here they sit inside ₹67,188 — roughly 4.5% of Meta spend — left on because placements default to automatic and nobody has looked.
Source: Meta Ads Manager, platform and placement breakdowns.

slides.title: The biggest placement is the worst one
slides.notes: Feed also has the best landing rate of the group at 35.87%, so it is not failing at everything. It is simply the most expensive way this account buys a lead.

blocks.text: Feed absorbs more than a third of the budget and returns the most expensive leads of the four major placements. Moving that budget to Instagram Reels at its own historical rate implies roughly 124 more leads for the same money.
Source: Meta Ads Manager, placement breakdown. Top five of 26 placements shown; these carry 99.6% of recorded leads.

slides.title: Facebook Stories: ₹427 a lead
slides.notes: Flagging the small sample size ourselves is what makes the rest of the deck credible. We are not cherry-picking a winner, we are pointing at an untested one.

blocks.text: FACEBOOK STORIES
The cheapest lead in the entire account, on 1.1% of the budget.

Thirty-seven leads from ₹15,787. It is a small sample and it may not hold at scale — which is exactly why it should have been tested properly a year ago. Instead it has been left as a rounding error while Feed spent thirty-five times as much at three times the cost.
Source: Meta Ads Manager, placement breakdown. 37 leads is a small base; treat as a test signal, not a proven rate.

slides.title: One account, four different jobs, no consistent strategy
slides.notes: The shared-ad-account point came from the client's own team. It explains a lot of the volatility and it is a prerequisite, not a nice-to-have.

blocks.text: Cheapest month, cost per 1,000 impressions
Dearest month, cost per 1,000 impressions
Spread

A 41-fold swing in media cost is not the auction moving. It is the account switching between reach buying and conversion buying without a plan, so Meta's learning resets every time. Add three resorts sharing one ad account and the algorithm never accumulates a clean signal for any of them.
Recommendation: Guhantara needs its own ad account, separated from the other two resorts, before any structural optimisation is worth doing.
Source: Meta Ads Manager monthly export, spend divided by impressions.

slides.title: The 51,289 conversions in this account are not bookings.
slides.notes: Be precise about what we know and do not know. We have not seen the conversion action definitions. What we have is four pieces of evidence from the output that make the current definitions indefensible.

blocks.text: THE CORE PROBLEM

Whatever they are — page views, phone-number clicks, scroll depth, an engagement event — they are being counted as the outcome, and every bid Google has made for 19 months has been optimised toward them.
The next four slides are the proof. Each one on its own would be a red flag. Together they mean the conversion column cannot be used to make a single decision.
We could not inspect the conversion actions directly — that needs account access.

slides.title: Who is already being asked for by name

rows: guhantara · guhantara resort · guhantara cave resort

blocks.text: Brand search volume is the cleanest read on who the market already wants. It also decides the Google split: how much belongs on your own name, and how much has to go and find demand that has never heard of you.
Volumes to be pulled from Google Keyword Planner, India, last 12 months. Fill before presenting.

slides.title: Proof one: 0.9% of the spend claims 67% of the conversions
slides.notes: Demand Gen is almost certainly firing a different, looser conversion action than Search. Until that is unpicked, blended account reporting is meaningless.

blocks.text: Demand Gen share of spend
Its share of reported conversions
Cost-per-conversion gap vs Search
A 76% conversion rate on a discovery campaign, at eighty paise a conversion, describes an event that fires on almost every visit. It does not describe somebody booking a room.
Source: Google Ads, campaign type report, 1 Jan 2025 – 29 Sep 2026.

slides.title: Proof two: one month holds two thirds of 19 months of conversions
slides.notes: If the client has been reported to on blended Google conversions, every number they have been shown since March is distorted by this one month.

blocks.text: March 2026 reports 34,488 conversions — 67.2% of everything the account has ever recorded — at ₹4.80 each.
Clicks jumped five-fold in the same month while cost fell. That is Demand Gen scaling, not demand for a cave resort tripling overnight.
Remove March and the account's whole conversion history changes shape. Any year-on-year report built on this is wrong.
Source: Google Ads, monthly report.

slides.title: Proof three: a 102.90% conversion rate
slides.notes: This is the hinge of the deck. Two independent platforms breaking the same way points downstream, to the shared website and measurement layer.

blocks.text: PROOF THREE · APRIL 2026
conversion rate. 142 conversions from 118 clicks.

More people converted than clicked. Like October's 133% on Meta, this is not a performance result — it is a measurement system reporting an event that does not require the click it is being credited to.
Both platforms are independently producing impossible numbers in the same period. That is not a coincidence — it points at the website and the pixel setup they share, which is the next section.
Source: Google Ads, monthly report. April 2026 also shows near-zero spend on both platforms.

slides.title: Proof four: the revenue column is not revenue
slides.notes: Without reliable values there is no return-on-ad-spend figure for Google, and any that has been reported was built on this.

blocks.text: For most of the account's life the conversion value is simply a copy of the conversion count — no rupee value assigned at all. For three months in 2026 someone assigned real values that look like room rates, then it reverted. The ₹8.37L of reported conversion value across the period is not comparable with itself, let alone with spend.
Source: Google Ads, monthly report, conversion value column.

slides.title: Under the noise, Google is getting more expensive every month
slides.notes: Rising cost per conversion plus falling volume plus a very high top-of-page share is the classic signature of an account leaning on a narrow set of terms.

blocks.text: Cost per conversion has risen 5.7× since February, on a conversion definition that is already too generous.
Clicks are falling while the absolute-top share climbs to 64–66%. The account is paying more to win a shrinking pool of searches.
Click-through rate in those months is 19–22%, far above a normal non-brand search campaign.
Source: Google Ads, monthly report.

slides.title: Is Google buying traffic Guhantara already owns?
slides.notes: Label this honestly. Overclaiming here would undermine the four proofs that came before it, which are solid.

blocks.text: A HYPOTHESIS, NOT A FINDING
The signals
What it means
Why it matters here
Click-through rate of 19–22%, absolute top-of-page share above 64%, and volume in the low thousands. Generic resort searches do not behave like this.
With 21,392 Google reviews, Guhantara has enormous organic brand demand. Paying to intercept it inflates the conversion count and hides how little new demand is being created.
Spend concentrated on the brand's own name. People searching "Guhantara" were coming anyway; the click is bought, not created.

To confirm: The Majority spends across jan01-2025 to sep29 2026 till date have been made across only two campaigns in Google that are two search campaigns and both have used brand keywords as the primary search keywords
Stated as a hypothesis because the campaign-level export does not contain search terms.

slides.notes: Setting the expectation that conversions will crash is essential. If we do not say it now, the first clean month looks like a disaster.

One URL serves day-out and rooms alike, so no page matches the search intent

Conversion value is a copy of the count in most months

slides.title: Both accounts are broken in the same place, and it is not in the accounts.
slides.notes: This is the argument the whole audit has been building toward. Slow down here.

blocks.text: SECTION FOUR
Data attribution not being proper
One URL serving two different products
A redirect to a booking domain the pixel cannot follow
No CRM to catch anything that survives
Four faults, one consequence: the moment a person leaves the advert, Guhantara loses sight of them. Everything in the last two sections is a symptom of this slide.

slides.title: Two Meta pixels are live on one website
slides.notes: Resolve to one pixel, one dataset, one set of standard events. Do it before any structural media change, or the before-and-after comparison is worthless.

blocks.text: Active Meta pixels on guhantara.com
Events double-count
One page view can register twice, inflating landing page views and conversions.
Optimisation splits
Signal is divided across two datasets, so neither learns quickly and neither is complete.
Nobody on the client side can currently say why, which of them the ad account optimises against, or what each is set to record.
Reporting cannot be trusted
This is a credible cause of the impossible 133% and 102.9% figures in both accounts.
Identified on the live site. Which pixel is canonical needs to be decided with the client.

slides.title: The chain breaks at the exact moment money changes hands
slides.notes: Step 5 is drawn as a ghost on purpose. It is the only step that produces revenue, and it is the only one the business cannot see.

blocks.text: The ad
guhantara.com
Book Now
Redirect
The booking
Meta or Google, tagged
Pixels fire — both of them
The visitor clicks through
secure-booking-engine.com — a different domain
Invisible. No pixel, no event, no attribution.
The pixel does not follow the visitor across the domain boundary, so every completed booking is unattributed.
Meta and Google are therefore optimising toward step 2 or 3 — a page view or a click — because that is the last thing they can see.
This single gap explains the ₹0.80 conversions, the impossible rates, and why nobody can name a cost per booking.
Booking engine: Djubo, served on secure-booking-engine.com.

slides.notes: We have not verified the embed is possible on their plan. Present it as the preferred route with a named fallback, not as a settled fact.

First action: confirm with Djubo whether their widget can be embedded on guhantara.com for this property and plan. Their product is described as an attachable widget, so this should be available — but it must be verified before we commit to it. If it cannot be embedded, the fallback is cross-domain tracking plus a server-side purchase event from the booking confirmation.
Either route restores the purchase event. The embed is cleaner; the fallback works if the embed is unavailable.

Steps 3, 5 and 6 do not exist today. Build those three and every number in this deck becomes decision-grade. Meta's Conversions API for Business Messaging does step 6 for click-to-WhatsApp ads, which is how most enquiries already arrive.
The loop runs left to right on the top row, then right to left on the bottom, back to the ad.

slides.title: There is no CRM. Here is what that costs.
slides.notes: The aggregator point is the commercial argument that lands with an owner, more than any marketing argument on this slide.

blocks.text: No attribution
No lead quality
Enquiries arrive by phone and WhatsApp — the only contact routes on the site — and nothing ties them to the campaign that caused them. Budgets get judged on clicks.
1,259 Meta leads exist as a number and nothing else. Which were serious, which booked, which were wrong numbers — unknowable.
No repeat business
No audiences
A corporate buyer who ran a good offsite last year is the cheapest lead the resort will ever have. Today nobody holds their name in a system that prompts a call.
Retargeting, exclusions, lookalikes and weekday offers all need a list of who enquired and who booked. That list currently lives in people's phones.

And underneath all four: 18,670 ratings on one booking aggregator is a dependency, not just a credential. The platform owns the customer, sets the price comparison and takes the margin. A CRM is how Guhantara starts owning its own demand.
The client confirmed no CRM is in place.

slides.title: What you would finally be able to see
slides.notes: Deliberately refusing to quote an industry qualified-lead benchmark is the honest move. Anyone can find a number online; nobody can find one for an underground cave resort in Bangalore.

blocks.text: Leads — every enquiry from every source, in one place
today: a number with no detail
MQL — right city, right party size, real contact details
today: invisible
SQL — reached, dates discussed, quote sent
today: invisible
Booked — room, day-out or offsite
today: invisible
With this you can price each stage: cost per MQL, cost per SQL, cost per booking — by channel, by campaign, by creative.
You can also send the booked stage back to Meta and Google, so they stop optimising toward the cheapest click.
Guhantara's own baseline sets the quality target. We would measure for one month before promising a percentage, rather than quoting an industry figure that may not fit a resort.

slides.title: Ads are running to a day-out page that does not load.

blocks.text: THE SINGLE MOST EXPENSIVE FAULT
The page returns too many requests and times out. Meanwhile paid traffic is being bought and sent to it.
This alone would depress the landing-page-view rate across the whole account. It is a strong candidate for a large share of the 66% of clicks that never arrive.
Day-out is the higher-volume product and the one the aggregators dominate. It is exactly the traffic Guhantara most needs to own directly.

slides.notes: The 44% figure is why retargeting and a content library matter more than a single burst campaign for the stay product.

blocks.text: The day-out buyer
The stay buyer
What both get
A family or a group planning a Sunday. Wants price per head, timings, the activity list, how far it is, whether children are catered for. Decides in a day.
A couple or a family booking a night underground. Wants room types, photographs of the interiors, rates, what is included, what the cave is actually like. Takes over a week.
The same URL. The same promotional homepage. Neither finds what they came for quickly, and the ad's promise is broken within two seconds of the click.

Beyond the conversion loss, this makes product-level measurement impossible. There is no way to say whether day-out or stay advertising works, because both land in the same place and neither fires a distinct event.
Four pages are needed, not one: day-out, stay, corporate offsite, weddings and events. Each with its own URL, its own event, its own ad set.

blocks.text: SECTION SIX
What we found
What it costs
What is missing

Creatives first launched in July are still running unrotated. Image and video quality is inconsistent across the set, and the messaging is built around the offer rather than around the person being shown it.
Frequency climbs, click-through falls, cost per lead drifts up. It is a credible part of why cost per lead moved from ₹236 in January to ₹698 by September.

Volume and test frequency are far below what this spend needs. No variant structure, no audience-specific messaging, no budget set aside for creative that might fail. Winners are never found because losers are never run.

Three fixes, in order: raise production quality on the cave itself, rewrite the messaging per audience against what each one actually responds to, and increase the number of creatives in market and the rate at which they are tested.

blocks.text: Why it matters commercially
What the reviews suggest
A rain dance is a ₹1,499 day ticket sold to a crowd. A cave is an ₹11,300 room, a ₹1,500-a-plate wedding and a corporate booking of the whole property.
Across thousands of reviews, the rain dance and the pool are cited more often than the cave. Guests are booking a water park that happens to be underground.
Why it happened
The advertising, the website and the booking engine all lead with activities and discounts. Guests are simply buying what they were sold.
Thrillophilia even lists the property as "underground location 10 m below ground, with water park" — the cave has become the adjective.

Rule two

A weekday offer that includes something the weekend crowd cannot get — a private amphitheatre slot, a guided tunnel trek, a facilitator, a spa credit — protects the rate and trains nobody to wait for a code.
From day one, report the two as separate lines. Otherwise a good weekend hides a bad Tuesday, and neither the client nor we can tell whether any of this worked.
